absent: Numeric file-type codes for the type mask, FIFO, socket and remaining file kinds, plus remaining permission and mode predicates.
Statx call convention, mask request semantics, error behavior, and filesystem obligations for unsupported fields.
Snapshot ioctl lifecycle ordering, privilege requirements, image format and concurrency rules.
Legacy sysctl call semantics, value encodings and permission checks for the enumerated nodes.
Locking, calling context and architecture override contracts for byte-swap helpers.

findings.text: User headers expose file-mode classifiers that mask a mode value with the file-type mask and test equality against the FIFO and socket type codes, succeeding only when the mode denotes that object kind.

Owner, group and other permission triples use octal encodings: full triples are 0700, 0070 and 0007; read bits are 0400, 0040 and 0004; write bits are 0200, 0020 and 0002; execute bits are 0100, 0010 and 0001.
Timestamp carrier holds signed 64-bit seconds, unsigned 32-bit nanoseconds, then a signed 32-bit reserved field, in that order.

Extended status record is 256 bytes with documented offsets: at 0x00 result mask, block size and attribute flags; at 0x10 link count, owner, group, mode plus spare; at 0x20 inode, size, block count and attribute support mask; at 0x40 four timestamps for access, creation, change and modification; at 0x80 special-device and containing-device major and minor pairs; at 0x90 mount identifier and direct IO memory and offset alignments; at 0xA0 subvolume and atomic-write minimum and maximum; at 0xB0 atomic segment maximum, read offset alignment, optimal atomic maximum plus spare; at 0xC0 reserved expansion through 0x100.

Query and result mask uses single-bit flags from 0x1 through 0x20000 for type, mode, link count, owner, group, three classic times, inode, size, blocks, birth time, mount id, direct IO alignment, unique mount id, subvolume, atomic-write fields and read alignment; the low eleven bits combine as basic stats 0x7ff, coverage through birth time is 0xfff, and the top bit 0x80000000 is reserved for future growth.

File attribute flags use hex bits 0x4 compressed, 0x10 immutable, 0x20 append-only, 0x40 no-dump, 0x800 encrypted, 0x1000 automount trigger, 0x2000 mount root, 0x100000 verity protected, 0x200000 DAX state, and 0x400000 atomic-write support.
Each user-visible header defines a distinct inclusion guard macro so repeated inclusion is idempotent.

Headers supply annotation and grouping helpers: a forced-inline alias, a union-based named member-group constructor with tag variants for C versus C++ linkage, two flexible-array declaration forms for zero-length versus true flexible members, no-op counted-by bounds annotations in native, little-endian, big-endian and pointer forms, and a nonstring marker that maps to the compiler attribute when available and otherwise to nothing.

SunRPC debug facility uses one-bit flags 0x1 through 0x800 for transport, calls, debug, NFS, auth, bind, scheduler, transaction, service transport, service dispatch, miscellaneous and cache, with 0x7fff enabling all facilities.

SunRPC-related legacy sysctl debug and slot identifiers form a sequence starting at 1 for RPC debug, NFS debug, NFSD debug, NLM debug, UDP slots, TCP slots, minimum reserved port and maximum reserved port.
Resume swap descriptor is packed and holds a kernel file offset followed by a 32-bit device number, with no padding.

Hibernation control uses ioctl magic value 3 with numeric operations 1 freeze, 2 unfreeze, 4 atomic restore, 5 free, 9 free swap pages, 11 suspend to RAM, 13 set swap area carrying the resume descriptor, 14 get image size, 15 platform support, 16 power off, 17 create image, 18 preferred image size, 19 available swap size and 20 allocate swap page, with maximum number 20.

Snapshot device exposes a hibernation lifecycle through distinct ioctl operations for freezing and unfreezing tasks, atomic restore, releasing state, managing swap pages and swap area, suspending, querying and creating images, platform support and powering off.

Compile-time byte-reordering primitives reverse byte order within 16, 32 and 64 bit values by masking and shifting each byte to its mirrored position, plus a 32-bit half-word exchange of upper and lower halves and a byte exchange inside each half.

Runtime byte-swap layer provides pure 16, 32 and 64 bit value swappers and 32-bit half-word and intra-half swappers that prefer architecture-specific implementations when defined and otherwise use the compile-time primitives, with 64-bit fallback combining two 32-bit swaps when only 32-bit support exists; word-size dispatch selects 64- or 32-bit swap by long width, constant-aware wrappers select compile-time versus runtime forms, pointer loaders swap the pointed-to value, and in-place variants store the swapped result back.

Legacy sysctl vector call allows at most 10 name components and passes a descriptor containing user pointers to the integer name path, component count, old and new value buffers with sizes, plus four unused words.

Top-level legacy sysctl categories are numbered 1 kernel, 2 virtual memory, 3 network, 4 proc, 5 filesystem, 6 debug, 7 device, 8 bus, 9 ABI and 10 CPU, with sparse extras 254 wireless, 5677 s390 debug, 7249 sunrpc, 9899 power management and 9898 FRV.
Second-level bus namespace holds ISA as 1; inotify limits are 1 maximum instances, 2 maximum watches and 3 maximum queued events.

Kernel sysctl numbers span 1 through 78 with gaps, covering system identity and build information, profiling, host and domain names, panic behavior, sparc and PPC machine controls, printk controls, module and device paths, accounting, real-time signal queue limits, shared memory and message queue limits, semaphores, sysrq, thread limits, random, overflow identifiers, hotplug, emulation warnings, core dump controls, tainted state, CAD process, PID maximum, power and alignment traps, ratelimits, pty, group limits, timer, NMI behavior, bootloader type, address randomization, dumpable behavior, spin retries, video flags, compat logging, lock depth and watchdog controls.

Virtual-memory sysctl numbers cover overcommit memory and ratio, page cluster, dirty background and ratio and writeback and expiry intervals, flush-thread count, pagebuf, huge-page count and group, swappiness, low-memory reserve, minimum free memory, maximum map count, block dump, cache pressure, legacy address layout, swap-token timeout, cache dropping, per-CPU list fraction, zone reclaim mode, minimum unmapped fraction, panic on out-of-memory, VDSO mapping and minimum slab fraction, with early numbers retained as unused spares.

Network family selectors number core 1 through DCCP 20 plus IRDA 412; random controls are pool size, entropy count, read and write thresholds, boot identifier and UUID numbered 1 to 6; pty controls are maximum and current count 1 to 2; ISA bus bases are memory base, port base and port shift 1 to 3.

Core network tunables number socket memory maxima and defaults, backlog, fastroute, message cost and burst, option memory maximum, hot-list length, divert version, congestion thresholds and states, device weight, connection queue maximum, budget, async event parameters and warnings 1 through 22; Unix tunables are destroy delay, delete delay and maximum datagram queue 1 through 3; connection-tracking timers and limits span maximum entries, TCP state timeouts and retransmission policy, UDP and ICMP and generic timeouts, bucket count, invalid-logging, SCTP state timeouts, entry count, IPv6 ICMP and fragment timeouts and thresholds, and checksum handling 1 through 32.

Extended status validity is governed by separate result and attribute-support masks: only bits set in the returned masks carry defined values, so readers must test those masks before interpreting optional timestamp, mount, alignment, subvolume and atomic-write members.
Snapshot ioctl command space is intentionally sparse with unassigned numbers between defined operations, so dispatch must reject unknown numbers rather than treating the range as dense.
